zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. The scan, not the index, governs this transcription. Data: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

runs.text: zaru toqinba toramo nezumito naru. Xix.

lines.note: Continues the preceding page's example: under the contrasting condition even a tiger becomes a rat. Nezumito, not OCR nozumito, agrees with the following Portuguese comparison; Xix. is the citation label.

runs.text: Estimando, & louuando a alguem de rato ſe

lines.note: Valuing and praising someone turns a rat into a tiger; the Portuguese sentence continues below. The historical louuando retains its printed u/v spelling.

runs.text: faz tigre, & deſeſtimãdoo de tigre ſe faz rato:

lines.note: Completes the positive comparison and reverses it: despising someone turns a tiger into a rat. The scan has faz tigre without an intervening a, and ends rato with a colon rather than the OCR's final s.

runs.text: aplicaſe aos homẽs os quaes tanto ſão quãto fa-

lines.note: The saying applies to people, whose standing depends on how others value them. Fa- continues as fazem below; the abbreviation tildes in homẽs and quãto remain unexpanded.
Completes fazem nelles, then introduces another sense of mochiiru: consuming something. Co- begins Portuguese comer on the following row, not a Japanese example.
Completes comer and adds drinking and taking medicines. These specify the consumption sense of Mochijru rather than the esteem sense in the preceding proverb.
Mochii is the noun for esteem or regard, directly glossed by Estima. It is a separate entry, despite its relation to the preceding verb.

runs.text: Aruore de cuja caſca piſada, fa-

lines.note: Mochi no ki is a tree whose crushed bark supplies an adhesive. The description continues below; it does not itself justify imposing a modern botanical species name.
Completes fazem and identifies the product as glue or birdlime. This connects the tree-name above with its practical use.
Mochiron denotes something clear and established beyond doubt. The gloss is more explicit than simply substituting the modern discourse translation of course.
Mochitsuke means having something as a habit or customary practice. The divided Portuguese habito has no clearly printed terminal hyphen here, so the baseline's bare ha is retained.

Completes habito and begins an example of the deep devotion one has customarily held toward the saints. The scan supports fucai-, corresponding to fukai, rather than OCR ſucai-; Iẽninye is retained as printed, with consonantal initial I.
Shinjin ni wa okotarazu completes the instruction not to neglect devotion. Mon. supplies the citation; de- begins the Portuguese noun continued on the next physical line.

runs.text: uação grande, que cuſtumastes ter aos ſanctos

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies the great devotion customarily held toward the saints. The printed de-/uação spelling and cuſtumastes are preserved rather than modernized.
Not failing in that devotion completes the Portuguese construction and explains Japanese vocotarazu. This short continuation remains a separate physical row.
Mochitsure describes several people carrying things together. The principal form is visibly ruru, not OCR turu, matching the verb's inflection.
Completes the definition of carrying something in company, then begins these people in the Japanese example. The final hyphen belongs to the physical division of fitobitoga.
These people carry uchigatana swords and masakari axes together. The case particle ga continues the preceding line, and the sentence proceeds to their disorderly entry below.
Midare iru describes entering in a disorderly crowd. Voi. is the upright citation label; the Portuguese begins the same account and divides Catanas across the line boundary.
Completes Catanas and says that the sword- and axe-bearing men entered in a throng. The printed entrarão is retained in this past narrative context.
Mochitsutae refers to holding or transmitting something over time. The following rows clarify inheritance through successive generations rather than a single act of carrying.

runs.text: por tempos, ou dedução de idades. ¶

lines.note: The possession extends through a succession of ages or generations. Mo- starts the Japanese example of an inherited household object on the following line.

Completes mochitsutayeta and refers to the ancestral possession of one's house. Giǔdai identifies the heirloom or hereditary possession; the printed gi spelling and unhyphenated Portuguese Cou are retained.

runs.text: ſa, ou peça que de muito tempo, & idades per

lines.note: Completes cousa and describes an object held over a long period through successive generations. The scan reads per at the line end, not OCR por.

runs.text: dedução hum tem em ſua caſa.

lines.note: Completes the explanation of an object preserved in one's household through a succession of generations. Dedução here concerns transmission, not a logical deduction.
Mochizuki is the full moon. The scan contains two successive z letters, Mochizzuqi, which the OCR reduced to one; the printed nasal abbreviation in Lũa is preserved.

runs.text: Caſa onde ſe vend,em ou fazem

lines.note: Mochiya is a shop where mochi are sold or made. The anomalous comma inside vend,em is visible in the print and is retained rather than moved to produce modern vendem, ou.
Mochis completes the Portuguese definition of the shop, using the Japanese food-name with a Portuguese plural ending. Its italic setting is retained; it is an embedded term, not a new headword.
Mochiyori means approaching while bringing something. The principal forms anticipate mochiyotta in the example; the Portuguese Trazẽdo keeps its printed abbreviation.
The example describes arriving with various kinds of sake and food. Enlargement supports mochiyotta with two t letters, consistent with otta above, rather than OCR mochiyota; Tac. is the citation.
The Portuguese translates the goods brought as much wine and various foods. Comeres is the historical substantive plural for things to eat.
Arrived or approached completes the translation of mochiyotta. This short verb is a genuine continuation of the preceding row.
Mōko is a fierce tiger, paraphrased in Japanese as takeki tora. The caron over o differs from the circumflex in Môcot below and is preserved independently.
Completes cruel, the second description of the fierce tiger. The upright S. marks written usage and is not part of the italic Portuguese adjective.
Mōkotsu denotes hair and bones, restated as ke and hone. The final t represents the checked Sino-Japanese ending; the circumflex and upright written-register label are retained.

runs.text: Couſa de deſgraça, ou que ſocedeo mal,

lines.note: Mokke describes something unfortunate or ill-fated in this gloss. The historical form ſocedeo is retained; the following adjective adds that it is hard to endure.
Insufferable completes the preceding description of something unfortunate. The old spelling inſofriuel remains literal rather than being normalized to a modern Portuguese form.
Mokkena gives an adjectival form with the same sense as Mocqe. Idem refers to the immediately preceding definition, not to an omitted gloss.
Mokkwa is identified only as a particular medicinal substance. The brief definition is retained without supplying an unprinted recipe or botanical identification.
Mokkai means doubting or suspecting someone in this written-register entry. The tilde in dalguẽ is an unexpanded abbreviation; S. is upright.
Moku is silence; moku suru is to remain or become silent. The example stays in roman type between the italic Portuguese glosses.
This separate moku entry means the grain or veins of wood, paraphrased as ki no me. It is unrelated to the preceding silence sense despite identical romanization.
Mokuba is a wooden horse, literally ki no uma. Initial v in vma represents the printed positional spelling of the vowel, not a consonantal modern v.
Mokubutsu is a wooden Buddhist image, paraphrased as kibotoke. The scan supports Qibotoqe with t, correcting OCR Qiboroqe; the Portuguese calls it an idol of wood.
Mokudai, equated with meshiro, is an official charged with supervision. The comma after i and printed per are retained; q̃ abbreviates the relative word without expansion.

runs.text: olhar, & vigiar pello q̃ lhe encarregão, como

lines.note: The official must watch over what is entrusted to him. The scan includes lhe, not OCR he, and the plural verbal form encarregão is preserved.

runs.text: por algũ lugar, pouoação, &c. ¶ Item, Nas

lines.note: A place or settlement is an example of the official's charge. Nas begins a further explanation continued at the top of column 2; OCR's fragmented type runs and Iiem are corrected to the continuous italic Item, Nas.

runs.text: varelas he officio como de miniſtro.

lines.note: Continues Nas from column 1: in temples the office is comparable to that of a minister or attendant. Officio has two f letters in the scan; the row is indented as a continuation, not a new entry.
Mokuzen is what lies before the eyes, paraphrased as me no mae. The Portuguese adds an extended meaning on the next line.
Something clear and manifest completes the extended sense of mokuzen. The provisional st allograph in manifesta is retained under the supplied typography guidance.
Mokujin is a wooden figure, literally a person made of wood. The Portuguese definition explicitly calls it a wooden statue.
Mokujiki is paraphrased in Japanese as eating only tree-fruits or nuts. This entire explanatory Japanese phrase remains roman and is not marked as a Japanese term embedded within Portuguese.

runs.text: Comer ſomente fruita, & couſas q̃ não ſão co-

lines.note: The Portuguese explains eating only fruit and things that are not cooked. Co- is the first part of cozidas, not a separate lexical item.
Completes cozidas and supplies mokujiki wo suru as the verbal example. No separate Portuguese translation is printed after that example.
Moku moku describes remaining quiet without speaking. The printed space between the repeated elements is retained.
Mokumoku to shite iru exemplifies being at rest and silent. The example joins the repeated elements, unlike the spaced headword above.
And silence completes the Portuguese description of the preceding state. It is a short continuation, not an independent definition.
Mokunen is given as an alternative to mokumoku; l means or. The unhyphenated example begins here and continues with to shite iru below.
Completes mokunen to shite iru. Idem refers back to the state of quiet repose and silence described in the preceding entry.
Mokuranji names a colour used for clothing. The gloss gives no further shade specification, so no modern colour identification is inserted.

runs.text: Mocurei. i, Cotoba naxini rei bacari ſuru.

lines.note: Mokurei means making a bow or salutation without words. The Japanese paraphrase says this directly; Portuguese fazer is divided without a visible hyphen after Fa.

runs.text: zer reuerencia no exterior ſem falar nada.

lines.note: Completes fazer and explains an outward reverence performed without speaking. This supplies the Portuguese equivalent of kotoba nashi ni rei bakari suru.
Mokuroku is a book's table or index, paraphrased as recording names. Taboada is the printed historical Portuguese term, not an arithmetic table in this context.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Rol de couſas que ſe mãdão de pre-

lines.note: A second sense is a list of things sent as presents. The abbreviation in mãdão and the divided presente are kept as printed.

runs.text: ſente, como barças de vinho, Sacanas, caua

lines.note: Completes presente and lists wine containers, sakana foods, and a horse continued below. Sacanas is a Japanese food-term adapted within the Portuguese sentence; the final caua has no supplied hyphen.

runs.text: lo, montante; ſe he rol de outras couſas, como

lines.note: Completes cavalo and adds a large sword. The scan's semicolon after montante introduces a contrast with lists of other objects, for which another Japanese term follows.
Lists of other articles are called chūmon. This roman Japanese cross-reference belongs within the Portuguese explanation, rather than constituting a new headword.

runs.text: Mocuromi, u, ǒda. i, Mocuſan ſuru.

lines.note: Mokuromi is equated with mokusan suru, calculating or estimating a position. The Portuguese verb lançar begins here; the scan's caron in ǒda is retained rather than regularized from inflectional expectation.

runs.text: çar bem as contas no jogo do Go acerca das riſ

lines.note: Completes lançar and explains calculating the lines or positions in the game of Go. Go is an embedded Japanese game-name; riſ continues below without an added hyphen.

runs.text: cas, pera ſaber quem ganharà, ou perderà.

lines.note: Completes riscas and states the purpose: determining who will win or lose. The scan reads contiguous pera, correcting OCR per a, and retains the grave accents on the future verbs.

runs.text: ¶ Item, per met. Lançar bem as contas ſo-

lines.note: The figurative sense extends the calculation to thinking something through carefully. The printed per met. label and the division of sobre are retained.
Completes sobre: calculate or think carefully about something and consider it well. This is the figurative extension from evaluating a Go position.
Mokusan means considering or counting the points, paraphrased as me wo kangayuru. The Portuguese again introduces the board's lines or squares.

runs.text: cas quadradas q̃ eſtão no taboleiro do Go, pera

lines.note: Completes riscas quadradas on the Go board. The scan supplies the missing q beneath the abbreviation mark and clearly names Go, not OCR Co; no modern account of scoring replaces the historical wording.

runs.text: ſaber quem ganha, ou perde. ¶ Per met.

lines.note: The calculation determines who wins or loses. Per met. then introduces a figurative example on the next row.

The Japanese example describes getting something right without calculation or effort. The visibly separate iy ateta and caron-marked monǒ are retained instead of being respelled from modern ii-ateta or historical morphology.

runs.text: cuidar, nem lançar conta, &c. i, Facillima-

lines.note: The Portuguese says the person succeeded without thinking or reckoning, then glosses this as very easily. Facillima- is divided across the physical line boundary.
Completes Facillimamente, the explanation of the effortless success in the preceding example. The short suffix remains its own physical row.
Mokusanmonō is separately entered and paraphrased as requiring no trouble or time. The printed caron and spacing are retained, rather than corrected from an expected grammatical analysis.
Without much business or labour completes the gloss. The upright X. is the dictionary's regional usage label, not a Japanese word in the Portuguese sentence.

runs.text: Certa mezinha feita de hũa erua,

lines.note: Mokutsū is a medicine made from a plant. The visible mark over the final u points downward like a caron, correcting OCR û; it does not imply an open/closed u distinction.
The plant is compared with ivy, in the printed historical form era. The gloss is a comparison, not sufficient evidence for identifying the exact modern species.

runs.text: Aruore de flores cheiroſas aßi cha-

lines.note: Mokusei is a tree with fragrant flowers. The scan reads Mocuxei, with a visible x, and Aruore, flores, aßi rather than the OCR's several malformed forms.
Completes chamada, stating that the fragrant-flowered tree bears the name Mocuxei. It contributes no additional botanical identification.
Mokuyō denotes tree leaves, paraphrased as ki no ha. The circumflex over o and historical f in fa are preserved.
Mokuyoku means washing the hair and bathing, explained by kami arai and yu aburu. The source's aburu is retained rather than modernized to a later form of the bathing verb.
Completes washing the hair and body, then starts the verbal expression mokuyoku suru. The following definition distinguishes a more specialized use.

runs.text: Lauar o corpo morto: posto que eſte he o

lines.note: Completes suru and defines it as washing a corpse. The initial Portuguese letter is L, not OCR I; the following concession explains the relation to the broader bathing sense.

runs.text: ſentido que ordinariamente corre, todauia nos

lines.note: The corpse-washing sense is said to be the one ordinarily current. Todauia introduces the qualification that follows in the next two rows.

runs.text: liuros, ou em praticas de homẽs que ſabem ſe

lines.note: Books and the discourse of learned people are the contexts in which the broader sense also occurs. The printed homẽs abbreviation remains unexpanded.
Completes the qualification: the term also has its first, general bathing sense. This is usage commentary rather than a third independent headword.
Mokuza is sitting silently; the Japanese paraphrase combines remaining silent with sitting. The Portuguese predicate continues below, and the long-s forms are retained occurrence by occurrence.
Without speaking completes the explanation of sitting silently. It remains a distinct short continuation line.
Mokuzō is a wooden image or statue, paraphrased as ki no katachi. The scan reads z before the caron-marked o, correcting OCR Mocuaǒ; the separate Mocuz- below is page furniture.
